newsitem.title: USA: Congress runs up against Oct.1 shutdown deadline.
newsitem.headline: Congress runs up against Oct.1 shutdown deadline.

text.p: Congress and the White House grappled Tuesday with the final details of major spending bill needed to avoid a government shutdown as Senate leaders warned next week's deadline may force them into a weekend session.

All sides said they were determined to avoid closing the government just before the Nov. 5 election. The government's new fiscal year starts next Tuesday, and without passage of the multibillion-dollar bill many agencies would be forced to close.

"I am not going to prolong this artificially just to keep us here," Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota told reporters. At the same time, Democrats will insist Republicans give details of the spending bill and amendments before they agree to allow a vote.

"I'm ruling out Democrats stopping a continuing resolution from passing simply to make a political point. I am not ruling out holding our ground," he said at a news conference at the end of Tuesday's session.

Republican leaders, faced with polls which show Democrats stand a chance of reclaiming control of at least the House, are anxious to send their lawmakers home to campaign. But Daschle noted that several Democratic senators face close races as well and his party wants to free them to campaign.

Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi, who sets the Senate schedule, said he has given lawmakers notice they should be prepared to work through the weekend, or to return Monday for final passage of the bill.
The largest item in the spending bill is the Defence Department's $245 billion. The rest will go to fund many federal agencies whose regular appropriations have not cleared Congress.

The negotiations so far have given President Clinton most of the $6.5 billion he wanted in extra domestic spending and to pay for antiterrorism programmes. Remaining to be decided are several policy issues, including an abortion-related issue concerning curbs on U.S. contributions to international agencies that use private funding for abortion services.
The House expects to begin debate on the spending bill, often called a continuing resolution or omnibus bill, by Thursday or Friday, said Republican Leader Dick Armey of Texas.
But as Armey said, "this is the last train out of the station," and members are eager to attach their special projects to the bill.

Lawmakers have said they will try to attach legislation to ban gun ownership by people convicted of domestic violence, to give banks some regulatory relief, and to give health plan physicians a clear right to discuss all available treatments wth patients.
Armey said he did not expect the government would be allowed to close, but that there could be disagreements before final resolution of all outstanding issues.
"There are always last-minute hitches in the get-along," he said.
